claim.pdf_says: 11.7.4   General rules  (a fourth-level clause heading, printed at the same typographic rank as 11.7.1 General, 11.7.2 General format and 11.7.3 Syntax rules)
claim.markdown_says: ## 11.7.4 General rules  (line 13070 of specs/ISO_COBOL.md - an h2, while its siblings are '### 11.7.1 General' at 13019, '### 11.7.2 General format' at 13024 and '### 11.7.3 Syntax rules' at 13037, and their parent is '## 11.7 METHOD-ID paragraph' at 13016)
claim.why_it_matters: 11.7.4 is promoted to the same heading rank as its own parent 11.7, so the general rules of the METHOD-ID paragraph detach from that paragraph in any generated TOC or outline-driven navigation and appear as a peer clause. Anchor-based lookups that walk the heading tree to find 'the rules belonging to 11.7' will not find them.

verdict.reasoning: Both quotations check out exactly, and the defect is genuine - but it is mislabelled and its stated impact is only half right. PDF SIDE (rendered E:/Temp/specrecon/v300/spec_p300.png and, for the siblings, E:/Temp/specrecon/v299/spec_p299.png at 300 dpi and read the glyphs). Page 300 (printed folio 270) prints, between syntax rule 9) and general rule 1), the bold heading '11.7.4 General rules'. Page 299 (printed folio 269) prints '11.7 METHOD-ID paragraph', '11.7.1 General', '11.7.2 General format' and '11.7.3 Syntax rules'. All five are set in the same bold face, same point size, same left margin - ISO does not vary typography by clause depth here, so depth is carried by the NUMBER, not by the type. The claim's phrase 'same typographic rank as 11.7.1/.2/.3' is therefore literally true but slightly misleading: 11.7 itself is printed identically too. What is unambiguous is that 11.7.4 is a fourth-level subdivision of 11.7 by ISO numbering, and it is the immediate successor sibling of 11.7.3. MARKDOWN SIDE (grep on specs/ISO_COBOL.md). Verbatim confirmed: 13016 '## 11.7 METHOD-ID paragraph', 13019 '### 11.7.1 General', 13024 '### 11.7.2 General format', 13037 '### 11.7.3 Syntax rules', 13070 '## 11.7.4 General rules'. So within one subclause the transcription uses h3 for .1/.2/.3 and h2 for .4 - an internal inconsistency, not a deliberate convention. The immediate control case confirms it: the exact analogue one page later, '### 11.8.4 General rules' at 13118, is an h3 under '## 11.8'. WHY IT IS NOT REJECTABLE AS MERE FORMATTING. Heading level in Markdown is the document's hierarchy, not cosmetics; a four-level clause number emitted as a peer of its own three-level parent is a structural fidelity break that a heading-tree consumer sees. It survives all four rejection tests except one label. WHAT THE CLAIM GETS WRONG. (1) Nothing is missing. The heading text '11.7.4 General rules' is present verbatim, the explicit anchor '' is present and correct at 13069, and every one of the seven general rules 1)-7) plus sub-items a)/b) transcribes faithfully against the render. kind='missing-heading' is a misnomer; this is a heading-RANK inversion. Id-based anchor lookup (#section-11-7-4) is unaffected - only tree-walking is. (2) The impact rationale is overstated in a way that would misdirect the fix. Demoting 13070 to '### ' does NOT reattach the rules to 11.7, because '## Page 300' at 13061 is itself an h2 that closes 11.7's subtree at the page boundary; an h3 at 13070 would nest under '## Page 300' instead. The page-marker scheme severs every cross-page clause subtree in this document regardless of this heading's level. (3) It is not an isolated page-300 fact. A doc-wide scan finds 2082 numbered headings, 586 of which sit at a level less than or equal to their parent's, and 322 of those fall within 12 lines of a '## Page' marker. The identical shape recurs at '## 11.10.4 General rules' (13583) whose siblings 11.10.1/.2/.3 are h3 and which likewise follows '## Page 311'. Page-boundary assembly is the mechanism.
verdict.corrected_description: Confirmed, but re-scope and re-label it. kind should be 'heading-level-inversion', not 'missing-heading': no text is missing - page 300 renders '11.7.4 General rules' and specs/ISO_COBOL.md carries that heading verbatim at line 13070 with a correct '' anchor, and all seven general rules transcribe faithfully. The real defect is that the fourth-level clause 11.7.4 is emitted as '## ' (h2) while its own parent '## 11.7 METHOD-ID paragraph' (13016) is also h2 and its three siblings 11.7.1/.2/.3 (13019/13024/13037) are '### ' (h3); the analogous 11.8.4 at 13118 is correctly h3. Two corrections to the impact statement: id-based anchor lookup still works, and demoting the heading to h3 alone would NOT reattach it to 11.7, because the '## Page 300' marker at line 13061 is itself an h2 that already severs 11.7's subtree at the page break - any real fix must derive heading level from the clause number AND stop emitting page markers as h2 headings. Finally, this is not a page-300 one-off: 586 of 2082 numbered headings sit at or above their parent's level, 322 of them within 12 lines of a page marker (e.g. the identical '## 11.10.4 General rules' at 13583 after '## Page 311'), so it should be ledgered as one instance of a systemic page-boundary heading-rank class rather than as an individual page finding.
